title: How Does a Dentist’s Age Factor Into Qualified Employer Sponsored Retirement Plans
html:
By Bruce Bryen, CPA, CVA

Since there are only 2 types of qualified employer sponsored retirement plans, it is important to make the correct choice for both the dentist and the dental practice when determining who will be responsible for the continuing tax deductible contributions to the plan. Factoring in a clinician’s age and the “normal retirement age” can have an impact on what benefit is the best fit.

This is not to be confused with the names of the retirement plans such as 401k, profit sharing, pension plan, etc. The actual plans are the defined benefit plan and the defined contribution plan.

The variations of these plans are the familiar names that the dentist may be used to hearing. The actual definition of the defined contribution plan such as a 401k is such that the deductible contribution to the retirement plan is defined. The rules allow a certain amount, which is defined, to be contributed to the retirement plan. Thus, the name, “defined contribution”.

The defined benefit plan is a much more complex and expensive plan. An actuary or someone or a firm acceptable to the IRS must calculate the benefit promised to the employees and based on the formula adopted by the plan, either add, subtract or do nothing to the pot of assets that the plan has accumulated in it. Based on the “normal retirement age” designated in the plan documents, the current age of the employees is factored into the formula to determine if the benefit at retirement, that is a fixed guarantee, is achievable with the degree of deductible contribution previously anticipated. As previously described, the amount may have to increase, decrease or remain the same based on the benefit formula.

Under what circumstances would a dental practice choose a defined benefit plan compared to a defined contribution plan?

An example of when a dental practice and its dentist owner would select a defined benefit plan would be if the dental practice has a reasonably steady income stream, the dentist is on the older side and the dentist’s taxes are increasing. The reasoning behind this scenario is that the “normal retirement age,” adopted in the plan documents may be on the low side. If the age of the owner is close to that “normal retirement age,” that means that the deductible retirement plan contribution must align with the current age of the owner compared to the expected retirement age.

Remember that the benefit for the owner and each employee is defined so that if the owner is hypothetically 60 years old and the expected retirement age is 65, the owner dentist has 5 years to fund the benefit for himself or herself. Compared to a 401k, as an example, where the contribution is defined, the deductible contribution into the defined benefit plan must be substantially higher since there are only 5 years to fund the benefit. The 401k has a limit on the contribution to the retirement plan since that contribution and not the benefit is defined. Profits and losses in the retirement plan also have a consequence to the deductible contribution since a loss for the year reduces the pot of assets available for distribution and the enabling of the retirement plan to meet its obligation of the funding for the benefit. This would force the dental practice to increase its contribution to the plan in order to overcome the deficiency in the pot of assets available to fund the defined benefit.

Suppose there is a profit in the retirement plan for the fiscal year that just ended?

The impact of a profit in the retirement plan for the fiscal year has the opposite effect on the deductible contribution compared to the impact of a loss. Since a loss would cause the assets in the retirement plan to decease, a profit would create an increase in the total assets available to fund the defined benefit and subsequently reduce the deductible contribution since the profit took the place of the full contributory amount.

The formula to determine the deductible contribution would be calculated to determine the new amount due that the dental practice had to pay into the retirement plan. This calculation would occur from year to year based on whether the retirement plan reported a profit or a loss for its fiscal year.

Discussing these points with a dental CPA or the actuary goes a long way in budgeting the dental practice cash flow. An example could be that if amounts needed to be paid into the retirement plan, a monthly budgeted amount could occur from the dental practice to the retirement plan. If an unusual increase in cash flow took place in the dental practice during a particular month, that increase could be paid immediately into the retirement plan to catch up on the potential underfunding. These various changes each year in the defined benefit plan cause additional services to be performed by the actuary or the dental CPA and of course cause the cost to keep the plan current more expensive. The benefits as one can see can result in additional material deductible tax deductions and contributions to the retirement plan. Today’s cost for the dental practice will increase the amount available for the dentist and other key employees of the dental practice when the time comes for those who will retire.

How does the dental practice owner choose between either employer sponsored qualified retirement plan?

The older the owner of the practice is, the more likely the defined benefit plan would likely be the best choice because of the shorter funding period as previously described. There should also be a consistently fairly high income being earned by the dental practice with high taxes due for the defined benefit plan to be worth its cost. The fewer and the younger the employees in the practice the better.

These are some of the areas to consider when making the determination of which type of plan to adopt for the dental practice. Constant communication with the dental CPA is important.
